methodological_questions: Does replacing one or more players in the offensive five shift shot mix (shot distance and three-point share) beyond what game state and team context explain?
Can a substitution-based design separate personnel effects from endogenous coach substitution decisions?
Is shot mix a valid and reliable outcome for detecting personnel effects, given that shot distance and type are mechanically linked and partly chosen by the offense?
Does the question as posed test a personnel effect, or does it assume the conclusion by treating a detected shot-mix change as proof that the design works?
evidence_establishes: The retrieval call returned no records (n_results = 0), so no earlier study from this project is available in this setting to support or contradict the question.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether changing the offensive five moves shot mix in NBA data.
The size, sign, or reliability of any personnel effect on shot mix.
Whether the substitution design has adequate power or freedom from confounding in these seasons.
Whether earlier work has already answered the question.
own_inferences: The question as posed is partly circular: a detected shot-mix change would show a personnel effect, but it would not by itself show that the design can detect personnel effects in general. A design check needs a known-null or placebo condition as well as a known-positive one.

Shot distance and three-point status are not independent outcomes of personnel. Shot type is largely determined by shot location, so a single shot-mix metric may conflate shooting zone with shot selection.

Substitutions are not random. Coaches change lineups in response to score, fatigue, foul trouble, and matchups, so a naive comparison of shot mix with and without a player will be confounded by game state.

The data (play-by-play with shot distance and results, substitution intervals, defensive matchup minutes) are sufficient for a within-team, game-state-adjusted comparison, but not for causal identification without additional assumptions.
uncertainties: Field-level detail for shot type and shot-clock timing is not confirmed here; the data catalog was not queried.
The number of lineup changes with enough offensive possessions on each side is unknown until the data are counted.
Playoff samples are much smaller than regular-season samples and may not support the same models.
Whether the 2022-23 to 2024-25 seasons show stable shot-mix patterns (rule changes, tracking-era shifts) is unknown.
The power calculation depends on an effect size that has not been established.

historical_effect.explanation: Retrieval returned no records, so no earlier finding changed the decision. The decision rests on the question's logic and the data description alone. The decision is to proceed only after the question is reframed as a testable estimand with a placebo and a pre-specified decision rule, not to run the design as the question is worded.

blocking_constraints.text: Coach-driven substitutions respond to score, fatigue, foul trouble, and matchups, which also affect shot selection. Without game-state and matchup controls, or an identification strategy, personnel effects cannot be separated from these drivers.

Shot-type and shot-distance categories are derived from play-by-play labels, and the three-point and distance buckets are mechanically related. The outcome definition has to be fixed before analysis to avoid circularity.
Within-team lineup contrasts on shot mix may be small in number and noisy per lineup. Playoff subsamples are likely underpowered.

prior_work.summary: No earlier work was retrieved, so no prior study can be cited. Whether this question has been answered elsewhere is unknown, not confirmed as no.

risks.text: Substitution timing depends on score, fatigue, foul trouble, and opponent lineup, all of which also drive shot selection.
Shot distance and three-point status overlap; a single shot-mix metric mixes shooting zone with shot selection.
Lineup-level contrasts within a team and season may have too few attempts to detect modest shot-mix shifts.
Many five-man combinations appear for few possessions, so lineup-specific estimates will be sparse.
Shot-mix shares computed over short lineup stints are noisy and may not be stable across stints or seasons.
If the design is validated only by a positive result, the test cannot distinguish a working design from a confounded one; a negative-control outcome and a placebo substitution are required.
Many lineup pairs, outcome definitions, and season splits invite selective reporting.
Shot-mix tendencies change across the 2022-23 to 2024-25 seasons, which can mimic or mask personnel effects if not modelled.
Using end-of-stint or whole-game statistics to define lineups or outcomes would use information not available at the time of the shot.

design.estimand: Within-team, game-state-adjusted change in offensive shot mix (share of attempts from three, and share of attempts from within 5 feet) when a specified player enters the offensive five, averaged over substitution events, with a placebo substitution contrast and a negative-control outcome to test the design.
design.unit: Offensive possession within a lineup stint, nested in team-game. Substitution events define stint boundaries.
design.sample: NBA regular seasons 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 as the primary sample. Playoffs as a secondary, descriptive sample only. Include only stints with a pre-specified minimum number of offensive possessions (set before analysis).
design.power: Compute minimum detectable effect before analysis for the chosen stint-length threshold, using team-season variance of shot mix. Report the minimum detectable shift in three-point share. If the MDE is larger than plausible personnel effects, report the test as underpowered rather than null.
design.controls: Team-game fixed effects; score margin, period, and game clock bins; home/away; opponent defensive matchup proxies from the defensive matchup minutes file; teammate composition via lineup fixed effects; and player-level random effects. Use only information available before each shot, not end-of-stint totals.
design.falsification: (1) Placebo substitution: randomly reassign the substitution timestamp within the same stint and confirm the estimated effect is near zero. (2) Negative-control outcome: test the same contrast on outcomes that should not depend on personnel, such as opponent shot mix or free-throw rate. (3) Pre-trend check: estimate effects in the possessions before each substitution and require them to be near zero. A design that fails any of these is not validated.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register one primary outcome (three-point share of offensive attempts) and one secondary outcome (close-range share). Apply Holm correction across lineup-pair families. Report all placebo and negative-control results alongside the primary estimate.
design.decision_rule: Claim a personnel effect on shot mix only if the primary estimate's 95% CI excludes zero, the placebo and negative-control contrasts are null, pre-trends are null, and the result holds across at least two of the three seasons. Otherwise report the result as inconclusive or as not validated.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files for 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular season and playoffs, as pulled on the analysis date (2026-11-02). Record the exact pull date, file versions, and the graph-database build used for derived possession records. Freeze the analysis file before estimation.

What confounders and power limits affect a substitution-based lineup design?
Is shot mix a valid and reliable outcome for detecting personnel effects?

You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.
